title: The Great Council at Horse Creek
subtitle: The Fort Laramie (Horse Creek) treaty council, North Platte River, 1851, with the Senate amendment of 1852–53
intro: In September 1851 the largest gathering the northern Plains had seen camped along the North Platte: perhaps ten thousand people of the Oceti Sakowin (Sioux), Tsitsistas (Cheyenne), Hinono'eino (Arapaho), Apsáalooke (Crow), Nakoda (Assiniboine), Mandan, Hidatsa and Sahnish (Arikara), with a Newe (Shoshone) delegation that the commissioners would not admit to the treaty. Congress had voted $100,000 to buy safe passage for the overland roads. The grass at Fort Laramie gave out within days, so on 5 September the whole council moved thirty miles downriver to the mouth of Horse Creek, in what is now western Nebraska. The people there called it the Great Smoke.

The record is almost entirely letters, newspaper dispatches, official reports, a treaty text and, for the nations, speeches taken down in English by the other side. There are few diaries. The fullest running account was sent from the 'Treaty Ground' to the St. Louis Missouri Republican by its editor, A. B. Chambers, who was also the council's secretary, and by B. Gratz Brown. Every Indigenous speech here reached print through an interpreter, often one named on the treaty, John S. Smith for the Cheyenne or John Pizelle for the Arapaho, and through reporters who called the speeches 'begging'. The book labels them as interpreted and gives them their own lines in the ledger.

Set side by side, the records do not agree on what was happening. Mitchell said the Great Father wanted no land; the map that De Smet and Jim Bridger drew on 12 September was presented as taking none, and Article 5 kept every nation's right to hunt and travel across the lines. Yet the Oglala objected at once that the lines cut off their country south of the Platte. The Lakota asked for a chief for each band and were given one head chief, Conquering Bear, chosen by Mitchell. The Shoshone rode five hundred miles to be told they were not parties. Upriver at Fort Union, the Swiss clerk Rudolph Kurz watched the Assiniboine refuse the chief the commissioners had made for them.

The nations' own records remember other things. Lakota winter counts name 1851–52 for the great issue of goods on the Platte, or for peace with the Crow, not for roads or boundaries. Hidatsa and Arikara witnesses in 1930, and a Crow elder in 2016, spoke of the treaty as a confirmation of their lands that was later broken. These are set out as positions, with no verdict.

The epilogue is administrative. On 24 May 1852 the Senate cut the promised annuities from fifty years to ten, with up to five more at the President's discretion, and made payment depend on the nations' consent. Fitzpatrick and the upper Missouri agent gathered assent in 1853 from every nation except the Crow. On 19 August 1854 Conquering Bear was mortally wounded near Fort Laramie when Lieutenant John Grattan's detachment fired on his camp over an emigrant's cow, and the peace the council had promised on the Platte ended.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Most dispatches are datelined 'Treaty Ground, near Fort Laramie'; the treaty itself is dated 'Fort Laramie, 17 September 1851' though it was signed at the Horse Creek camp. Lakota and Dakota winter counts run from first snow to first snow and name each year after a single event, so 'the winter of 1851–52' covers roughly autumn 1851 to autumn 1852; such entries are sorted as 1851 with precision 'year'. The English year-names are those recorded by Garrick Mallery and William Corbusier in the 1870s and 1880s.

eyes.name: David Dawson Mitchell
eyes.role: Superintendent of Indian Affairs at St. Louis, aged about 45; former fur trader of the American Fur Company on the upper Missouri; chief US commissioner
eyes.where: St. Louis, then Fort Laramie and the treaty ground at the mouth of Horse Creek
eyes.vantage_label: chief commissioner who ran the council
eyes.form: speeches as reported in the press; official report
eyes.authenticity: His speeches survive as taken down by the Missouri Republican's men on the ground (published October 1851), not in an official verbatim minute. His official report was printed with the Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1851.
eyes.bio: Mitchell had spent years in the upper Missouri fur trade before becoming superintendent, and knew several of the nations at first hand. At Horse Creek he set the camps, gave the opening and closing speeches, drew the boundaries onto a map with De Smet and Bridger, and chose head chiefs when the nations would not. His words are those of the man who wanted the roads open and believed he was offering protection.

sources.title: Leslie Wischmann, 'Separate Lands for Separate Tribes: The Horse Creek Treaty of 1851' (WyoHistory.org)
NMAI Native Knowledge 360, 'Horse Creek Treaty' (quotes Missouri Republican and the 1851 Annual Report)

eyes.name: Thomas Fitzpatrick
eyes.role: Indian agent for the Upper Platte and Arkansas since 1847, aged about 52; former mountain man and guide, known to the Plains nations as Broken Hand; co-commissioner
eyes.where: Fort Laramie and Horse Creek; then with a delegation to Washington; back on the Platte in 1853
eyes.vantage_label: co-commissioner and agent who had urged the council
eyes.authenticity: His reports are in the Office of Indian Affairs correspondence (National Archives RG 75) and the printed Annual Reports; the treaty's printed note cites his 1853 Upper Platte file for the tribes' assent to the Senate amendment.
eyes.bio: Fitzpatrick had guided the first wagon companies west and had argued since 1847 that the overland roads were eating the Plains nations' grass, timber and game. He co-signed the treaty, took a delegation east, and in 1853 carried the Senate's shortened annuity term back to the nations for their assent. He died in Washington in early 1854.

sources.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 17 Sept 1851 (Kappler text with amendment note)

eyes.name: Pierre-Jean De Smet, S.J.
eyes.role: Belgian-born Jesuit missionary based at St. Louis, aged 50
eyes.side: Society of Jesus; travelling with the upper Missouri delegations
eyes.where: Fort Union, overland via the Powder River country and Red Buttes, then Horse Creek
eyes.vantage_label: missionary, mapmaker and baptiser on the treaty ground
eyes.authenticity: His letters on the council were printed in his Western Missions and Missionaries (1863) and in Chittenden and Richardson, Life, Letters and Travels of Father Pierre-Jean De Smet (1905). Some were written in French and translated; the printed texts were edited, so they are paraphrased here.
eyes.bio: De Smet led a party of about thirty-five, including chiefs of the Assiniboine, Hidatsa, Arikara, Mandan and Crow, from Fort Union to the council. He helped draw the boundary map, preached, and recorded baptisms by camp. His letters are warm about the people and blunt about their hunger.

sources.title: De Smet's 1851 map of the Upper Great Plains (Library of Congress)

eyes.name: Missouri Republican correspondents (A. B. Chambers and B. Gratz Brown)
eyes.role: Adam B. Chambers, editor of the St. Louis Missouri Republican, served as secretary of the council; B. Gratz Brown, a young St. Louis lawyer, signed the treaty as a witness
eyes.where: the treaty ground at Horse Creek
eyes.vantage_label: secretary and press on the treaty ground
eyes.authenticity: Dispatches datelined 'Treaty Ground, near Fort Laramie' (9, 10 September and later) appeared in the Missouri Republican in October 1851 and were reprinted elsewhere. They are the fullest running record of the speeches, but they are one side's English, written by men who sometimes scorned what they heard; which of the two wrote each dispatch is not always clear.
eyes.bio: With no official verbatim minute surviving in print, the newspaper dispatches are the nearest thing to council minutes. They recorded the camps, the parades, the counting of coups and the speeches through interpreters, alongside the writers' own sneers at 'begging speeches'. Read with that bias in view, they preserve what many nations' speakers said.

sources.title: Transcription of 1851 dispatches, 'Treaty Ground, near Fort Laramie, September 9, 1851'

eyes.name: Jacob H. Holeman
eyes.role: US Indian agent for Utah Territory, newly arrived from Kentucky
eyes.side: United States (Utah superintendency, under Governor Brigham Young)
eyes.where: the Sweetwater east of South Pass, then Fort Laramie and the council
eyes.vantage_label: agent who brought the Shoshone, then was told they did not count
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Commissioner Luke Lea are in National Archives RG 75, Microcopy 234 (Utah Superintendency); OCR transcriptions are online through the University of Utah. Some pages lack their opening or date.
eyes.bio: Holeman gathered the Newe (Shoshone, called Snakes in the record) on the Sweetwater and brought sixty headmen some five hundred miles to the council, only to find Mitchell regarded them as outside his superintendency and not parties to the treaty. His letters are the view from the trail's western end, where Mormon settlement was the complaint.

sources.title: Holeman to Lea, letter on the Shoshone trip (OCR)
Utah superintendency letter on the Laramie council's effect (OCR)

eyes.name: Percival G. Lowe
eyes.role: Enlisted man in the 1st US Dragoons, aged about 23; part of the escort
eyes.where: Fort Laramie and the treaty ground
eyes.authenticity: Five Years a Dragoon ('49 to '54) and Other Adventures on the Great Plains was published in 1906, more than fifty years after the council; vivid but written from memory.
eyes.bio: Lowe served in the dragoon escort at the 1851 council and later became a wagon master and Kansas businessman. His memoir gives the soldier's view: horses, guard duty, and an admiring account of the Shoshone arrival. Its dates and dialogue should be read as recollection.

sources.title: Review of the 1991 University of Oklahoma Press edition (Western Historical Quarterly, via eScholarship)

eyes.name: Bark, or Bear's Feather
eyes.where: the Cheyenne camp at Horse Creek
eyes.authenticity: Known only from the newspaper dispatch of 10 September 1851, in English taken down by the Missouri Republican's men; the Cheyenne interpreter named on the treaty was John S. Smith.
eyes.bio: Bear's Feather spoke for the Cheyenne on the day the Crow arrived. As the dispatch rendered him, he spoke of the buffalo growing scarce and called the day a great medicine day. Nothing else in his own words is known to survive.

eyes.name: Beka-chebetha (Cut Nose)
eyes.role: Hinono'eino (Arapaho) chief; signed the treaty as Beh-kah-jay-beth-sah-es
eyes.where: the Arapaho camp at Horse Creek
eyes.authenticity: His speech survives only in the newspaper dispatch's English; the Arapaho interpreter named on the treaty was John Pizelle (Poisal). His signature is a mark beside a name written by the secretary.
eyes.bio: Cut Nose asked that whites stay out of Arapaho country or pay for the game they drove away, and said that if they did he could rest without guarding his horses. He was one of three Arapaho signers.

eyes.name: Matȟó Wayúhi (Conquering Bear)
eyes.role: Sicangu (Brulé) Lakota warrior, named head chief of all the Lakota (Sioux) by the commissioners
eyes.where: the Lakota camps at Horse Creek; later near Fort Laramie
eyes.vantage_label: the head chief the commissioners made
eyes.authenticity: His acceptance speech survives only in the Missouri Republican's English; the Sioux interpreter named on the treaty was C. Campbell. He is generally identified with the first Sioux signer, Mah-toe-wha-you-whey.
eyes.bio: The Lakota bands would not choose a single chief, so Mitchell chose Conquering Bear, a Brulé not yet regarded as a leader even in his own band. He accepted reluctantly. Three years later, on 19 August 1854, he was mortally wounded near Fort Laramie when Lieutenant Grattan's detachment fired on his camp over a strayed emigrant's cow.

eyes.name: Mato Witko (Crazy Bear, Ours Fou)
eyes.role: Nakoda (Assiniboine) leader; signed the treaty as Mah-toe-wit-ko and was named Assiniboine chief
eyes.where: Fort Union, the journey with De Smet, Horse Creek, then back on the upper Missouri
eyes.vantage_label: Assiniboine signer made chief by the commissioners
eyes.form: words reported by traders and a clerk; letter (as dictated)
eyes.language: Nakoda, rendered into English and German
eyes.authenticity: Seen through Kurz's journal, Denig's report and the National Park Service's summary of them; a letter to De Smet survives in translation. None of it is in his own hand.
eyes.bio: Crazy Bear was the first Assiniboine to volunteer for the dangerous ride through Lakota and Blackfeet country with De Smet. While he was at the council the Blackfeet killed his son. Back home he kept to the treaty's peace, refused to retaliate, and told his people he had not sold their lands.

sources.title: Fort Union Trading Post NHS, 'Crazy Bear'
Denig, Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Rudolph Friedrich Kurz
eyes.role: Swiss painter working as a clerk at Fort Union, aged 33
eyes.side: Swiss; employee of the American Fur Company
eyes.where: Fort Union, at the mouth of the Yellowstone
eyes.vantage_label: clerk at the upriver post, hearing the news
eyes.authenticity: His journal was translated by Myrtis Jarrell and published by the Bureau of American Ethnology as Bulletin 115 (1937); later reissued as On the Upper Missouri (2005). Modern translation, so paraphrased only.
eyes.bio: Kurz had come west to paint Native people and spent the 1851–52 season as a clerk at Fort Union, sharing quarters with Crazy Bear for part of the winter. His journal watched the treaty arrive upriver as a set of appointed chiefs and promised goods, and recorded his doubts about chiefs made by outsiders.

sources.title: Fort Union Trading Post NHS, 'Crazy Bear' (quotes Kurz's dated entries)

eyes.name: Lakota winter-count keepers (American Horse, Cloud Shield, Lone Dog, White-Cow-Killer)
eyes.role: Keepers of pictographic year-records for Oglala, Minneconjou and other Lakota and Dakota bands
eyes.where: Lakota and Dakota camps on the northern Plains
eyes.language: pictographs with Lakota and Dakota explanations, rendered into English
eyes.authenticity: Published by Garrick Mallery in 'Pictographs of the North American Indians' (Fourth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1886), with explanations collected by Mallery and by army surgeon William H. Corbusier; the English names are the collectors' renderings of what keepers told them.
eyes.bio: A winter count names each year after one memorable event, drawn on a hide and explained aloud by its keeper. Several counts name the winter of 1851–52 for the great issue of goods on the Platte; others name it for the peace made with the Apsáalooke (Crow). They show what the council meant at home: the goods and the peace, rather than the boundary lines.

sources.title: Mallery, Pictographs of the North American Indians (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Wolf Chief
eyes.role: Hidatsa elder, a child at the time of the council; testified in the 1930 claims case of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara
eyes.authenticity: Testimony recorded in 1930 for the Indian claims case before the US Court of Claims; quoted on the National Museum of the American Indian's Horse Creek page. It is memory and community knowledge, not an eyewitness account of the council.
eyes.bio: Wolf Chief was a well-known Hidatsa elder who worked with anthropologists and spoke for his people's land claims. In 1930 he testified about how the Hidatsa came to understand the Fort Laramie lands had been taken from them. With Arikara witness Red Bear's testimony that the treaty had confirmed the lands to the three tribes, it gives the upper Missouri nations' later reading.

eyes.name: Grant Bulltail
eyes.authenticity: Interview recorded by the National Museum of the American Indian in August 2016 for its Native Knowledge 360 treaty lessons; modern, so paraphrased only.
eyes.bio: The Apsáalooke rode nearly 800 miles to the council and were the one nation that never gave its assent to the Senate's amendment. In 2016 Bulltail described what the Crow wanted from Horse Creek: recognition of their country and a way to keep intruders out of it.

entries.headline: First Assiniboine to volunteer for the ride south
entries.digest: When De Smet looked for upper Missouri leaders to go to the council, Crazy Bear was the only Assiniboine who offered at first. The route ran through Lakota and Blackfeet country, and others held back. Two more agreed only once he had committed.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union, 'Crazy Bear' (month inferred from De Smet's departure date)

entries.headline: Superintendent leaves St. Louis; the goods lag behind
entries.digest: Mitchell set out from St. Louis for the council called for 1 September. At Kansas Landing late in July his train of presents was still sitting on the river dock, which was to cost him weeks of waiting on the Platte.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, Horse Creek Treaty essay, timeline

entries.headline: De Smet's party starts overland for the Platte
entries.digest: De Smet left Fort Union with about thirty-five men: scouts, wagon masters and chiefs of the Assiniboine, Hidatsa, Arikara, Mandan and Crow. Ahead lay hundreds of miles of country none of the delegations had crossed together in peace.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, 'Father De Smet in Wyoming'

entries.place: Powder River country to Red Buttes
entries.headline: Lost, misdirected, then on the trail he knew
entries.digest: The party backtracked several times before entering the country below the Bighorn Mountains, where his companions named a lake for him. Three Crow guides led them astray, but they struck Red Buttes on the North Platte, and from there De Smet knew the road to Fort Laramie.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, 'Father De Smet in Wyoming'

entries.place: Sweetwater, about fifty miles east of South Pass
entries.headline: A talk with the Shoshone on the Sweetwater
entries.digest: Holeman met the Newe (Shoshone) on the Sweetwater, hired an interpreter and guide, and told them of the council. They chose sixty headmen to speak for the whole nation. He thought bringing them in would benefit the Indians, the country, and the emigrants who crossed Shoshone land.
entries.source_note: Holeman to Lea, OCR page (University of Utah, NARA M234)

entries.headline: Mitchell reaches Fort Laramie ahead of his wagons
entries.digest: Mitchell arrived at Fort Laramie two days before the council date. Thousands of people and horses were already gathering, and the presents he needed to open proceedings were still far down the trail.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, timeline

entries.headline: News that the southern nations will not come
entries.digest: Fitzpatrick told Mitchell that the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache had refused to come so far north into the country of their enemies. The council would be a northern one; the southern Plains nations had to be dealt with separately two years later.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, timeline

entries.headline: Sixty Shoshone headmen arrive and are told they are outsiders
entries.digest: Holeman brought his Shoshone delegation in to Laramie on 1 September. He then learned that Mitchell's instructions did not cover the Shoshone, who would receive presents but not be parties to the treaty. He argued in writing that they belonged to his superintendency and asked Washington for clearer orders.
entries.source_note: Holeman to Lea, OCR page (University of Utah); Commissioner's Report 1851 p. 10

entries.headline: The dragoon remembers the Shoshone riding in
entries.digest: Lowe recalled the arrival of the Shoshone among camps of their old enemies, and the discipline with which they rode in and held themselves while tension ran high. Writing half a century later, he said the soldiers took them to their hearts.
entries.quote: Every dragoon felt an interest in that tribe
entries.source_note: Lowe, Five Years a Dragoon (1906), as quoted in the eScholarship review (p. 67 of the 1991 edition); date from Holeman

entries.headline: The grass is gone; the council moves thirty miles east
entries.digest: The pony herds had stripped the grass around the fort, so after consulting the tribes the commissioners moved the whole gathering about thirty miles down the North Platte to the mouth of Horse Creek. Mitchell laid out where each nation, the traders and the interpreters would camp.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, timeline; NPS Fort Laramie history, Part I ch. VIII

entries.headline: De Smet arrives at sunset
entries.digest: De Smet reached the treaty ground at sunset after five weeks on the trail, met by Jim Bridger and carried to the grounds in Robert Campbell's carriage. His upper Missouri chiefs followed the next night.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, timeline and narrative

entries.headline: Opening speech: not traders, not land-seekers
entries.digest: A cannon shot called the nations to an arbour where Mitchell opened the council. As reported, he said the Great Father wanted nothing they owned, but asked for safe passage on the roads, posts along them, peace between the nations and fixed territories, in return for goods each year.
entries.quote: We do not come to you as traders
entries.source_note: Missouri Republican, as quoted in WyoHistory.org and Twain's Geography

entries.headline: The plains covered with people coming to council
entries.digest: The correspondent watched the nations converge on the arbour after the signal gun. That afternoon the Cheyenne made reparation to the Shoshone for men they had killed, covering the dead with gifts and returning scalps. The Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara and Assiniboine came in that night.
entries.quote: the whole plains seemed to be covered with the moving masses
entries.source_note: Missouri Republican, as quoted in WyoHistory.org

entries.headline: Cheyenne soldiers parade; coups are counted
entries.digest: About a hundred young Cheyenne soldiers rode in as a war party with painted horses, charging and wheeling with precision, their families behind. Men then stood to count their coups with a drumbeat for each deed, some counting twenty-five or thirty. That evening the Sioux gave a dog feast for the whites.
entries.source_note: Dispatch datelined Treaty Ground, 9 September 1851 (fmoran.com transcription)

entries.headline: The Crow arrive after nearly 800 miles
entries.digest: At nine the cannon was fired and the flag raised. The Apsáalooke (Crow) rode in with their interpreter Robert Meldrum after a journey of nearly 800 miles; Mitchell met them beyond the camp, smoked with them and set their camp near his own. The correspondent admired their horsemanship and dress.
entries.source_note: Dispatch of 10 September 1851 (fmoran.com transcription)

entries.headline: Sioux speakers ask for many chiefs and for grass
entries.digest: Mitchell asked for answers to his proposals and heard the Sioux first. A Brulé chief (rendered 'Terre Blue') said each band wanted its own chief and that his people were poor. Big Yankton asked why travellers were not given grass of their own, and Painted Bear said they could not understand white men's ways or words. The writer dismissed these as 'begging' speeches.
entries.quote: We want a chief for each band.
entries.source_note: Dispatch of 10 September 1851; speeches as interpreted (Sioux interpreter on the treaty: C. Campbell)

entries.headline: A Cheyenne speaks of the buffalo
entries.digest: Bear's Feather, as rendered by the interpreter, said the buffalo had once been plentiful in Cheyenne country and were becoming scarce. He called the day a great medicine day.
entries.quote: The buffalo used to be plenty in our country.
entries.source_note: Dispatch of 10 September 1851; speech as interpreted, probably by John S. Smith

entries.headline: Keep off our land, or pay for the game
entries.digest: Cut Nose, as rendered in English, asked that whites keep out of Arapaho lands or pay for the game they drove off; if that were done he could sleep without watching his horses. An old grey-bearded Arapaho then turned to his own people and told them they were given over to their white brothers.
entries.quote: I will sleep sound, and not have to watch my horses.
entries.source_note: Dispatch of 10 September 1851; speech as interpreted, probably by John Pizelle (Poisal)

entries.headline: Drawing the nations' lands onto a map
entries.digest: At Mitchell's request De Smet and Jim Bridger, with the traders' help, drew a map of the nations' territories, trying to follow traditional homelands. They worked until twilight. De Smet's map of the upper Plains, made that year, survives in the Library of Congress.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org, narrative; LOC item 2005630226

entries.headline: The map is shown; the Oglala object
entries.digest: Mitchell laid the map before the nations and said the lines were not meant to take any of their lands away. The Oglala protested that their hunting grounds reached south of the Platte; Mitchell answered that any nation might enter another's country if it came in peace. The territories were accepted.
entries.quote: not intended to take any of your lands away
entries.source_note: Missouri Republican, as quoted in WyoHistory.org

entries.headline: A Sunday of baptisms, camp by camp
entries.digest: De Smet baptised mostly children and recorded them by camp: 239 Oglala, 305 Arapaho, 253 Cheyenne, 280 among the Brulé and another Sioux band, 56 in Painted Bear's camp, and 61 of mixed descent, about 1,194 in all. He wrote that the people heard him readily and admitted their faults.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org (De Smet's figures); total is the sum of those figures

entries.headline: Mitchell names one chief for all the Sioux
entries.digest: The Lakota had not chosen a single leader, which was not their way. Mitchell named Conquering Bear, a Brulé warrior, as head chief of all the Sioux, and the bands accepted the choice reluctantly.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org (Monday after the opening)

entries.headline: The new head chief promises to try
entries.digest: As the Missouri Republican rendered his reply, Conquering Bear accepted with misgivings, promising to do right by the whites and hoping they would do right by his people. He was taking on authority over bands that had not given it to him.
entries.quote: I will try to do right to the whites
entries.source_note: Missouri Republican, as quoted in WyoHistory.org; speech as interpreted; day of the speech inferred from the appointment

entries.headline: Treaty signed by commissioners and twenty-one chiefs
entries.digest: Mitchell and Fitzpatrick signed for the United States; twenty-one chiefs of the Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Assiniboine, Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara made their marks. Six interpreters, army officers, Robert Campbell and B. Gratz Brown witnessed. Article 7 promised $50,000 a year in goods for fifty years.
entries.source_note: Treaty text (Kappler); WyoHistory.org

entries.headline: Crazy Bear makes his mark for the Assiniboine
entries.digest: Crazy Bear signed as Mah-toe-wit-ko, first of two Assiniboine signers, with Culbertson named on the treaty as interpreter for the Assiniboine. Far upriver, during his absence, Blackfeet raiders killed his son.
entries.source_note: Treaty signatories (Kappler); NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear'

entries.headline: The wagons arrive at last
entries.digest: The commissioners' supply train rolled in on the evening of the 20th, to general joy in camps where people had waited nearly three weeks, with the grass failing and food running short.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org; Smithsonian Magazine (VanDevelder)

entries.headline: Uniforms, swords, then the goods
entries.digest: Mitchell raised the flag, fired the cannon and dressed each chief in a general's uniform with a gilt sword before distributing the goods band by band. Each band took its share and moved away, and the camps began to break up.
entries.source_note: WyoHistory.org; Smithsonian Magazine

entries.headline: The rush to the distribution
entries.digest: De Smet described men, women and children hurrying to the grounds in confusion and their finest dress as the goods were laid out. Elsewhere in his letters he wrote that many of the nations he saw were in absolute destitution, and he backed a land grant for families of mixed descent as a way to keep them together.
entries.source_note: De Smet's letters, as quoted in WyoHistory.org

entries.headline: Who pays for bringing the Shoshone?
entries.digest: Holeman wrote to Lea that Mitchell had promised in his circular to cover the costs of bringing nations to the council, then ruled that the Shoshone, some five hundred miles from home, were not under his superintendency. Governor Young agreed, and Holeman had no funds, so he drew on the Department.
entries.source_note: Holeman to Lea, 22 Sept 1851 (OCR, NARA M234 reel 897)

entries.headline: Waiting for the bourgeois to return from Laramie
entries.digest: Kurz noted that a portrait was to be finished before Alexander Culbertson came back from Fort Laramie. At the upriver post the council was still a distant errand that had taken the chief trader and several leaders away.
entries.source_note: Kurz journal, as excerpted in Denig, Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri (BAE 46th Report)

entries.headline: The proceedings appear in print
entries.digest: The Missouri Republican published the council proceedings, including Mitchell's speeches. Among his words, the Great Father asked the nations for the right of free passage for his people over the roads through their countries.
entries.quote: the right of free passage for his White Children over the roads
entries.source_note: NMAI Native Knowledge 360 (Missouri Republican, 27 Oct 1851)

entries.headline: Crazy Bear comes home a chief by appointment
entries.digest: Kurz recorded that Crazy Bear had come back appointed chief of the Assiniboine by 'Uncle Sam', the commissioners. The traders at the fort were pleased; Denig thought it the best choice that could have been made.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear' (Kurz, 31 Oct 1851)

entries.headline: A clerk's doubt about chiefs made by outsiders
entries.digest: Kurz reflected that appointing chiefs whom the nations had not chosen themselves only bred jealousy among rivals. It was the same problem the Lakota had raised at Horse Creek when they asked for a chief for each band.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear' (Kurz, 15 Nov 1851)

entries.headline: Neither Assiniboine nor Crow recognise him
entries.digest: Kurz noted that most Assiniboine bands did not accept Crazy Bear's new title and that the Crow were hostile to him. The treaty's head chief held his rank in the eyes of the United States more than in the eyes of his own people.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear' (Kurz, 26 Nov 1851)

entries.headline: The superintendent's report on the treaty
entries.digest: Mitchell's report, printed with the Commissioner of Indian Affairs' Annual Report, explained the treaty's provisions and his hopes for it. It also set out his view, common among officials then, that mixing with white settlers was the only way the Indian nations could survive.
entries.quote: an intermixture with the Anglo-Saxon race is the only means
entries.source_note: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1851, as quoted by NMAI; exact date of Mitchell's own letter not seen

entries.headline: The Shoshone come home trusting, the Ute left out
entries.digest: A Utah superintendency report said the Shoshone who went to Laramie had been well received by the other nations and returned trusting the government more. The writer regretted that the Utah nations had not been made parties to the treaty and urged a similar council in the territory the next year.
entries.source_note: Utah superintendency letter, OCR page (University of Utah); author and date not shown on the page, attributed to Holeman from context

entries.headline: Delegates meet the President
entries.digest: Fitzpatrick escorted delegations of Arapaho, Cheyenne and western Sioux, with Oto and a few Iowa, to Washington. Commissioner Lea addressed them at his office, they were introduced to President Fillmore, and they spent an hour in full dress at the Commissioner's house at Mrs Lea's invitation.
entries.source_note: Press report transcribed on fmoran.com (undated Monday); Cheyenne delegates chosen 9 Sept per WyoHistory.org

entries.headline: 'First annuities at the mouth of Horse Creek'
entries.digest: The American Horse count names the winter for receiving the first annuities at the mouth of Horse Creek. Its picture is a one-point blanket standing for the dry goods, ringed by marks for the people who came to get them.
entries.quote: They received their first annuities at the mouth of Horse Creek.
entries.source_note: Mallery 1886, Corbusier Winter Count No. I, Plate XLVI (count-keeper identification per Mallery's numbering)

entries.headline: 'Many goods were issued to them at Fort Laramie'
entries.digest: A second count collected by Corbusier names the year for the many goods issued at Fort Laramie, the first the people had received. White-Cow-Killer's count calls it the Large-issue-of-goods-on-the-Platte-River winter.
entries.quote: Many goods were issued to them at Fort Laramie.
entries.source_note: Mallery 1886, Corbusier Winter Count No. II and White-Cow-Killer's count

entries.headline: 'Peace made with the Crows'
entries.digest: Three counts published by the Bureau of Ethnology name the same year for peace with the Crow. One shows two men with different hairstyles exchanging pipes. Mallery's note adds that the peace was, as usual, broken almost at once.
entries.source_note: Mallery 1886, Bureau of Ethnology counts Nos. I–III, Plate XXVI; No. I is usually identified as Lone Dog's count

entries.headline: Crazy Bear and a peace that will not hold
entries.digest: Kurz recorded Crazy Bear's distress that a northern Assiniboine band refused to make peace with the Blackfeet. The man who had signed for peace between the nations could not make all his own bands keep it.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear' (Kurz, 12 Feb 1852)

entries.headline: The Senate cuts the annuities from fifty years to ten
entries.digest: Ratifying the treaty, the Senate amended Article 7 so that the $50,000 a year in goods would run for ten years, with up to five more at the President's discretion, instead of fifty. The change needed the nations' assent, and the next payment was held back until it was given. The task of getting it fell to the agents, Fitzpatrick for the Platte.
entries.source_note: Commissioner's Report (Senate amendments of 24 May 1852 to Art. 7); Kappler amendment note

entries.headline: 'I have not sold your lands'
entries.digest: Speaking to the assembled Assiniboine, Crazy Bear told them he had not sold their lands at Laramie and that they should accept the annuity goods. Many were frustrated that he would not let them retaliate against the Blackfeet.
entries.source_note: NPS Fort Union 'Crazy Bear' (as reported by traders)

entries.headline: Assent gathered, except from the Crow
entries.digest: Fitzpatrick and the upper Missouri agent obtained the nations' assent to the shortened term. The printed treaty notes that every nation assented except the Crow, and the Commissioner reported the upper Missouri nations had agreed promptly where the agent could reach them.
entries.source_note: Kappler note citing Upper Platte file C 570, 1853; Commissioner's Report (c. 1852–53)

entries.headline: A Hidatsa elder on how the land was lost
entries.digest: Testifying in the claims case, Wolf Chief described how the Hidatsa came to realise that the lands recognised for them at Fort Laramie had been taken by the government. Arikara witness Red Bear testified in the same case that the treaty had made known that the lands belonged to the three tribes.
entries.source_note: 1930 Court of Claims testimony, as quoted by NMAI Native Knowledge 360

entries.headline: What the Crow wanted from Horse Creek
entries.digest: Interviewed by the National Museum of the American Indian, Grant Bulltail said the Apsáalooke went to the council to secure their country and keep out the miners, settlers, trappers, traders and ranchers. He framed the treaty as a boundary the Crow meant to enforce.
entries.source_note: NMAI Native Knowledge 360, interview August 2016

claims.claim: Shoshone choose sixty headmen to go to the council and speak for the whole nation
claims.evidence: Holeman to Lea (NARA M234, Utah; OCR University of Utah)

claims.claim: Mitchell rules the Shoshone outside his instructions: presents, but no place in the treaty
claims.evidence: Holeman to Lea; Commissioner's Report 1851 p. 10

claims.claim: The Great Father wants none of their land, horses or robes; asks roads, posts, peace and boundaries for annual goods
claims.evidence: Missouri Republican, Oct 1851, as quoted by WyoHistory.org

claims.claim: Cheyenne cover the Shoshone dead with gifts and return scalps, making peace between them
Brulé speaker asks for a chief for each band, not one for all the Sioux
Big Yankton: travellers destroy the grass and timber; give them grass of their own
The buffalo, once plentiful in Cheyenne country, are growing scarce
Whites should stay off Arapaho lands or pay for the game they drive away
Boundaries are 'not intended to take any of your lands away'; any nation may enter another's country in peace
claims.evidence: Missouri Republican, via WyoHistory.org; treaty Art. 5 reserves hunting and passage rights

claims.claim: Accepts the head chieftainship: will try to do right by the whites and hopes they will do right by his people
Treaty signed: peace among the nations, US roads and posts, US protection, territories, head chiefs, $50,000 a year for fifty years
Chiefs given uniforms and gilt swords; first goods distributed band by band
claims.evidence: Missouri Republican and De Smet, via WyoHistory.org

claims.claim: The year is remembered as the first great issue of goods, and as the peace with the Crow
claims.evidence: Winter counts in Mallery 1886 (American Horse, Cloud Shield, White-Cow-Killer, BAE Nos. I–III)

claims.claim: Senate amends Art. 7: annuities for ten years (plus up to five at the President's discretion), not fifty, subject to the nations' assent
claims.evidence: Commissioner's Report (amendments of 24 May 1852); Kappler note

claims.claim: Assent to the amendment obtained from all the nations except the Crow
claims.evidence: Kappler note citing Upper Platte C 570, 1853

claims.claim: The Hidatsa came to realise the Fort Laramie lands had been taken from them by the government
claims.evidence: Court of Claims testimony, quoted by NMAI

convergences.label: The Shoshone ride in to Fort Laramie
convergences.note: Holeman's letter records the arrival and the bureaucratic snub that followed; Lowe, writing fifty years later, remembers only their bearing and the soldiers' admiration. The agent's grievance and the trooper's romance describe the same sixty men.

convergences.label: The council opens at Horse Creek
convergences.note: Mitchell's speech promised that the United States wanted nothing the nations owned; the correspondent saw a plain covered with people; De Smet, arrived the night before, was bringing in the upper Missouri delegations that came after dark.

convergences.label: The Crow arrive; the nations answer Mitchell
convergences.note: The same dispatch carries a Brulé's call for a chief for each band, a Cheyenne's warning about the buffalo and an Arapaho's demand to be paid for game. The writer heard begging; the speakers, as rendered, were describing grass, game and land under pressure from the roads.

convergences.label: The map is drawn and presented
convergences.note: De Smet and Bridger drew the lines on 12 September; Mitchell presented them the next day as taking no land. The Oglala objection about the country south of the Platte shows the lines were read as limits from the start.

convergences.label: Head chiefs by appointment
convergences.note: Mitchell made Conquering Bear chief of all the Sioux; Conquering Bear accepted with a conditional promise. Two months later at Fort Union, Kurz wrote that making chiefs this way bred jealousy, as Crazy Bear's case was showing.

convergences.label: The treaty is signed
convergences.note: The commissioners' text and the chiefs' marks record the same act. For Crazy Bear it came with news of his son's death at Blackfeet hands; for Cut Nose it followed his demand that Arapaho game be paid for.

convergences.label: The great distribution
convergences.note: The commissioner recorded uniforms and swords, the missionary a crowd in its finest dress, and the winter counts the whole year as the first issue of goods. On the Lakota side the year was remembered for the goods, not the treaty clauses.

convergences.label: Upriver, the appointed chief comes home
convergences.note: Kurz's journal follows Crazy Bear from welcome at the fort to rejection by most Assiniboine bands and by the Crow, through the winter of 1851–52.

ties.note: Co-commissioners who signed the treaty together; Fitzpatrick had pressed for the council since 1847.
Crazy Bear rode with De Smet's party from Fort Union to the Platte; he later wrote, through others, to De Smet about the vanishing buffalo.
Mitchell asked De Smet, with Bridger, to draw the boundary map that he then presented to the nations.
Holeman brought the Shoshone; Mitchell ruled them outside his superintendency and refused their expenses, and Holeman complained to Washington.
Both watched the Shoshone delegation come in at Fort Laramie, one as its agent, the other in the dragoon escort.
Mitchell appointed Conquering Bear head chief of all the Lakota bands on 15 September 1851.
Cut Nose's speech survives only because the Missouri Republican's men took it down in English.
Bear's Feather is known only from the same 10 September dispatch.
Kurz drew Crazy Bear three times and shared quarters with him at Fort Union in the winter of 1851–52, learning Assiniboine words from him.
Mitchell's distribution of 21 September became the year-name in several Lakota winter counts.
Fitzpatrick gathered assent to the shortened annuity term; the Crow, whose later views Bulltail describes, were the one nation recorded as never assenting.
Fitzpatrick was agent for the Upper Platte, where Conquering Bear's people lived; both men died in 1854, Fitzpatrick in February and Conquering Bear after the Grattan fight in August.

threads_out.note: The country south of the North Platte that the 1851 treaty recognised for the Cheyenne and Arapaho was cut down at Fort Wise in 1861 and again at Medicine Lodge in 1867, where many of the same nations met US commissioners once more.

The council was called to protect the overland roads that the gold rush had crowded after 1849; Big Yankton's complaint that travellers destroyed the grass and timber describes the traffic of the California trail.
The Mandan and Hidatsa who signed in 1851 were the nations whose villages sheltered Lewis and Clark in the winter of 1804–05; their territory in Article 5 ran along the same stretch of the Missouri.

Crazy Bear's warning that his people's children must learn new ways as the buffalo disappeared anticipates the collapse of the herds that hung over Treaty 6, which Nakoda (Assiniboine) bands in Canada also joined.

images.caption: The manuscript map associated with the council, showing the country and nations of the northern Plains as De Smet understood them in 1851. The lines drawn at Horse Creek with Bridger were based on this kind of knowledge.
